title: Drift-O-Meter Build Board
phase: Phase 2 — engine tuning against the reworked simulator, app screens next
summary: An iPhone app (Expo SDK 57, TypeScript) that judges real drifting from the gyroscope, accelerometer and GPS and turns a run into a cinematic replay. Each piece is built by its own agent and judged by a separate fresh-context critic that re-runs the code and looks at the actual output, never the builder's summary. The reference bar is Need for Speed and Tokyo Drift.
verification: This build machine is Linux: it cannot compile or run the iOS binary. The engine is pure TypeScript and is exercised by tests against a physics simulator with ground truth.
The UI is the real app bundle, built for web, run in Chromium and screenshotted by the harness; critics judge those screenshots and videos, never the builder's summary.
What only a phone can verify (real CoreMotion units, haptics, 100 Hz timing, GPS latency in the field) is listed as on-device checks in the final hand-off.

pieces.name: Sensor simulator
pieces.verdict: Critic found the ground truth teleporting at both ends, a sign-flipped loose-mount gyro, bang-bang throttle and three-tone vibration. All rewritten; 14 physics tests now assert the kinematic identities themselves.
pieces.note: Kinematic drift driver on two tracks, phone-mount model, gyro bias, vibration, GPS latency/noise, ground truth

pieces.name: Mount calibration
pieces.verdict: Rebuilt against the new sensor model: lever arm, leaning OS gravity, timestamp jitter. Test suite being written now.
pieces.note: Phone frame → vehicle frame from gravity and forward acceleration

pieces.name: Slip-angle estimator
pieces.verdict: Six targets marginally missed after the sensor rework; the lever arm and the receiver-filtered GPS course are being modelled explicitly.
pieces.note: Kalman fusion of gyro heading, lateral-g kinematics and GPS course

pieces.name: Drift detection
pieces.verdict: Retuned: the drift now starts where the flick that initiated it started, not where the slide crossed a threshold. Entry latency 604 ms down to 224 ms, transition counting 70 % up to 100 %.
pieces.note: Entry / sustain / transition / exit state machine

pieces.name: Scoring & style
pieces.verdict: Complete: 33 tests green. Angle × duration × speed, multipliers, chains, callouts, S–D grade.
pieces.note: Angle × duration × speed, multipliers, callouts, S–D grade, consistency

pieces.name: Track & laps
pieces.verdict: Complete: laps from a derived start gate, reference lap refined every lap, corners, cross-lap consistency.
pieces.note: GPS → local map, lap gate, corners, lap-to-lap consistency

pieces.name: Signal integrity
pieces.verdict: Retuned: loose-mount cues renormalised to a scale measured over 384 rigid configurations. A rigid mount scores at most 0.12, a rattling cradle 0.20 to 0.66, a hand 0.80 to 1.00.
pieces.note: Loose-mount detection, physics plausibility, GPS quality gating

pieces.name: Replay scene
pieces.verdict: Failed: the frames are a telemetry map, not a replay. The ghost was the car itself for half the run, one bad sensor sample killed the camera for good, and a 70° near-spin looked identical to a 15° slide.
pieces.note: Session → timeline, glow trail, camera, ghost

pieces.name: Engine pipeline
pieces.verdict: Wiring every module into one object the app talks to, plus recorded sessions for the screens to load.
pieces.note: One object the app talks to: sensors in, live frames and a scored session out

pieces.name: App foundation
pieces.verdict: Theme, Barlow Condensed type, navigation, Skia running on web, sensor adapters, and a Playwright harness that shoots the real app bundle.
pieces.note: Theme, fonts, navigation, Skia on web, sensor adapters, screenshot harness

pieces.name: Live drive HUD
pieces.note: Angle, g-meter, speed, score combo, callouts, glow

pieces.name: Replay screen
pieces.note: Track map, trail, scrubber, camera modes

pieces.name: Calibration flow
pieces.note: Mount guidance with live sensor feedback

verdicts.summary: A fresh-context critic wrote its own probes, rendered 26 extra frames including the ones a builder would avoid, and measured the images pixel by pixel. The model underneath is clean and well tested. What it draws is not a replay.
findings: The ghost car was numerically identical to the car being watched for 47 % of the replay, and its gap readout divided a distance by instantaneous speed, so a constant 3.9 second gap flickered between 3.9 and 4.5.
A single NaN speed sample permanently destroyed the camera: 1203 of 1800 frames went non-finite and never recovered, which on the phone is a blank screen for the rest of the session.
Markers from lap one were never retired, so every label on lap two was drawn on top of its own twin, making the same corner look like it had six transitions.

Nothing escalated. The intensity ceiling was set to exactly the simulator peak, so a forced 70° slide rendered pixel for pixel like a 15° one, and the gold reserved for extreme angles appeared in none of the 26 frames.
The world window measured 74 to 91 percent pure background and the car occupied 0.151 percent of it, about 5 mm on a real phone.
Fourteen of 23 text elements were below the iOS minimum size, and the points numeral was the biggest thing on screen instead of the angle.
The telemetry strip showed the final score and grade in the very first frame, so the replay opened by revealing its own ending.

verdicts.summary: A fresh-context critic re-derived the simulator physics from its own output and failed it. Everything downstream is tuned against this ground truth, so a wrong simulator means a wrong app.
findings: Ground truth teleported 0 → 46 km/h in one 10 ms sample at the start and snapped 33° of heading at the end of every lap.
The hand-held sway fed the gyroscope with the wrong sign, so loose-mount data was physically impossible.
The advertised under-damped initiation flick was dead code; every drift began with a 1255°/s² kink no car can produce.
Linked corners were never actually linked, so the signature transition happened once per lap instead of throughout.
Vibration was three pure tones, which a downstream filter could trivially notch out instead of learning to be robust.
The track did not match its own description: the "right-hand sweeper" was a left, the chicane had no left-right.

log.text: Environment checked: Linux, no Swift toolchain and Swift downloads blocked; npm and PyPI reachable. Stack decided: Expo SDK 57 + TypeScript engine + Skia, verified via web build in Chromium.
Shared engine contracts written (types, unit conventions, frames). App-foundation agent launched.
Simulator producing 100 Hz phone-frame IMU + 1 Hz GPS with latency for two tracks; first plots inspected.
Six engine agents launched in parallel: mount calibration, slip estimator, drift detector, scorer, track model, replay scene. Critic protocol written.

User pointed at driftmeter.app: its stack (phone-only sensors, stationary zeroing, 60 Hz, EKF gyro+GPS course, physics-signature validation) confirms the estimator design; we go to 100 Hz, full mount-rotation calibration and a signal-integrity module, with a video-game presentation.

Simulator rewritten against the critic verdict: continuous start and roll-out, feint plus bounded yaw acceleration on initiation, linked corners, broadband vibration, phone lever arm, leaning OS gravity, per-seed GPS latency with a filtered course.
Session limit paused four agents mid-tuning. Everything they had written was already on disk.
Restarted: mount, slip, detector and integrity are being re-tuned against the new simulator, and the pipeline that joins every module is being wired.
Replay visuals failed their first critique at 4.5 out of 10 with four severity-one defects. The full findings went back to the builder with before-and-after measurements required for each one.

Detector and integrity are green again, 51 tests, with every original target still asserted at its original value. A critic is now checking whether the four judgement modules together would agree with a human drift judge.
